title: A Jewish tailor from Reno reinforced pants with rivets, and with Levi Strauss patented them in 1873

trailer.text: According to NPR, jeans originate with Jacob Davis, a Latvian-born Jewish immigrant tailor who worked in Reno, Nevada, and who added metal rivets at the stress points of the pants to strengthen them.
According to NPR, Davis teamed up with Levi Strauss, a dry goods merchant in San Francisco, and the two obtained a U.S. patent on May 20, 1873.
According to Biography.com, Strauss's family was also Jewish, and in Bavaria it suffered religious discrimination because of this.
According to the Smithsonian, production began immediately, and according to NPR, jeans have since become a staple in Western fashion.

stations.title: A tailor from Riga and a merchant from Bavaria

paragraphs.text: According to Levi Strauss & Co., Jacob Davis was born in Riga, Latvia, in 1831.
According to the genealogist Kathleen Clemence, he was born in a town near Riga, and his original name was Jacob Youphes.
According to his testimony, he arrived in New York by ship in March 1854.
According to the company, he became an American citizen in 1871.
According to J. Weekly and NPR, Davis was Jewish.
According to the Smithsonian, Levi Strauss was born in Bavaria.
He was 24 and a newly minted American citizen when he set sail for San Francisco in 1853 to open a branch of his brother's dry-goods business.
According to Biography.com, his family in Bavaria suffered religious discrimination because it was Jewish.
According to his testimony, before working on pants, Davis had used rivets to attach straps to horse blankets.
According to the historian Lynn Downey, unriveted denim had been worn as work wear for decades before.
According to the fashion historian Emma McClendon, denim had been worn for generations by enslaved Africans and their African American descendants.

stations.title: A woman asks for strong pants

paragraphs.text: In January 1871 in Reno, Nevada, the wife of a laborer asked Davis to make a pair of cheap, durable pants for her ill husband.
Her husband was a large man sick with dropsy, and he could not get a pair of pants to fit him.
According to IPWatchdog, the husband was a woodcutter.
She paid Davis three dollars and asked for strong pants, because her husband generally tore his clothes while working.
Davis also told of this woman in his court testimony.
According to his testimony, Davis saw rivets lying on the table, and then thought to use them to attach the pockets.
According to the Smithsonian, he strengthened the pants with copper rivets at the pocket openings.
He did this to help a customer who complained about constantly torn pockets.
According to NPR, the rivets were placed at the stress points of the pants.
According to Biography.com, he also put rivets on the front fly seam.
According to IPWatchdog, Davis charged only $3 for the first pair.
After he had made several pairs, larger orders began to come in, because other laborers noticed the quality of the pants.
According to San Diego Jewish World, before long he had filled orders for 200 pairs.
According to the historian Lynn Downey, Davis wanted to mass manufacture the pants, but he needed a business partner.
According to Clemence, each patent application cost him $68, a large sum at the time.
According to Clemence, his wife Annie, mother of five children under the age of 7, put her foot down.
According to J. Weekly, in 1872 Davis, a regular Strauss customer, sent a letter to Strauss.
According to History.com, Davis wrote to Strauss about his method of making work pants with metal rivets on the stress points.
He suggested that Strauss fund the application and that the two get the patent together.
According to J. Weekly, Davis did not have the money to file the application.
According to IPWatchdog, Strauss agreed and paid the patent fees.
According to Levi Strauss & Co., Davis also asked him to help with large-scale manufacture.
According to the National Archives, the fabric came from Strauss's store, and Strauss was the first person Davis told about the invention.
According to the research of the genealogist Clemence, Strauss was not Davis's original fabric supplier.
On May 20, 1873, Jacob Davis received patent #139,121 for an improvement in fastening pocket-openings.
The improvement was a metal rivet or eyelet at each edge of the pocket opening, to prevent the seam from ripping at those points.
According to IPWatchdog, the rivets were copper, and the reinforcements proved extremely desirable and durable.
In the patent description, the declarant acknowledged that rivets had already been used to secure seams in shoes, as shown in patents from 1867 and 1872.
Davis also wrote there that he did not claim broadly the fastening of seams by means of rivets.
Strauss and Davis decided to become partners, and they patented the invention under both their names.
According to the Smithsonian, production began immediately.
According to the US National Archives, Strauss and Davis decided to partner and patented the invention for fastening pocket-openings under both of their names.

stations.title: From home seamstresses to blue denim

paragraphs.text: According to Clemence, as soon as the patent was granted Davis went to work at Levi Strauss & Co. as, essentially, the plant manager, and he worked there until his death.
According to J. Weekly, Strauss brought him to San Francisco to oversee the first West Coast manufacturing site.
According to History.com, at first seamstresses worked for them out of their homes.
At first, seamstresses working out of their homes were employed, but by the 80s of the 19th century Strauss had already opened his own factory.
According to Clemens, at first the "overalls" were sewn from white cotton fabric, and in 1874 denim became the preferred fabric.
According to Biography.com, the pants were first made of heavy canvas.
The company then switched to denim dyed blue, reportedly to hide stains.
According to J. Weekly, production number (Lot No.) 501 was first issued in 1881.
According to the Smithsonian, the patent expired in 1890, but the popularity of the riveted trousers became an American legend.
According to NPR, jeans have since become a staple in Western fashion.

stations.title: A marker on Virginia Street, and an inventor's family

paragraphs.text: According to Levi Strauss & Co., in 2006 a marker was placed at the site of Davis's tailor shop on Virginia Street in Reno.
According to San Diego Jewish World, the marker is at 211 Virginia Street, downtown.
According to the marker, Davis decided to put copper rivets at the stress points to strengthen the pants.
The marker also says that Davis needed a business partner and therefore approached Levi Strauss.
According to the Levi's company historian, Davis also invented a button fastened with a screw, a type of steam-powered canal boat, and an ironing and stretching board for tailors.
According to San Diego Jewish World, Annie and Jacob Davis had eight children, two of whom died in infancy.
On January 31, 1874, Davis and Strauss filed a suit for patent infringement against A. B. Elfelt et al., claiming damages of $20,000.
On February 10, 1875, the court decided in their favor, but awarded them only $2,000.
According to an IPWatchdog writer, a patent application written this way would not be granted today, because its description is too open-ended.
